commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Sadhana (Prerequisite for Higher Yoga)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that the physiological state of stability (asana) and the regulation of vital intake (ahara) are foundational steps before advancing into higher yogic practices like pranayama. It reflects the philosophical principle that the mind cannot be stilled if the body is restless or improperly nourished.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This serves as a core psychological principle in modern wellness, recognizing the inextricable link between gut health (mitahara) and mental stability, a concept increasingly validated by modern neuro-gastroenterology.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practices prescribed are 'Asana-sthairya' (attaining steady posture) and 'Mitahara' (measured and nutritious diet) to facilitate 'Indriya-jaya' (mastery over senses).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Krama' or systematic progression: The bhashya highlights that yogic progress follows a specific 'Krama' (order), where 'Asana-siddhi' (postural perfection) acts as the 'Adhikara' (prerequisite) for 'Pranayama'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: From a psychological perspective, this verse underscores the importance of 'environmental and physiological priming.' Establishing routines and controlled input is seen as a prerequisite to cognitive focus or meditative depth in any modern professional or therapeutic setting.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: ‘प्रयोजनमनुद्धिश्य न मन्दोऽपि प्रवर्तते’ इति महदुक्तेः प्रयोजनाभावे प्रवृत्त्यभावात् प्राणायामप्रयोजनमाह - चले वात इति । वाते चले सति चित्तं चलं भवति । निश्चले वाते निश्चलं भवेत्, चित्तमित्यत्रापि सम्बध्यते । वाते चित्ते च निश्चले योगी स्थाणुत्वं स्थिरदीर्घजीवित्वमिति यावत् । ईशत्वं प्रप्नोति । ततः तस्माद् वायुं प्राणं निरोधयेत् कुम्भयेत् ॥ २ ॥
commentaries.text: ‘प्रयोजनमनुद्धिश्य न मन्दोऽपि प्रवर्तते’ इति महदुक्तेः प्रयोजनाभावे प्रवृत्त्यभावात् प्राणायामप्रयोजनमाह - चले वात इति । वाते चले सति चित्तं चलं भवति । निश्चले वाते निश्चलं भवेत्, चित्तमित्यत्रापि सम्बध्यते । वाते चित्ते च निश्चले योगी स्थाणुत्वं स्थिरदीर्घजीवित्वमिति यावत् । ईशत्वं प्रप्नोति । ततः तस्माद् वायुं प्राणं निरोधयेत् कुम्भयेत् ॥ २ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Recognizing the dictum that 'even a fool does not act without a purpose,' and since there is no action without a purpose, the author explains the purpose of Pranayama through the verse 'cale vate...'. When the breath moves, the mind becomes unstable. When the breath is steady, it becomes steady (the word 'citta' is applied here as well). When both the breath and the mind are steady, the Yogi attains 'sthanutva' (immobility, implying a state of enduring longevity). He gains mastery. Therefore, one should restrain—i.e., perform Kumbhaka (breath retention) on—the Vayu (prana).

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Citta-vritti (Control of Mind via Breath)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse posits an inseparable link between the physiological state of breath and the psychological state of the mind. By controlling the rhythm of Vayu (prana), one effectively arrests the fluctuations of the citta, facilitating a state of internal stillness necessary for higher meditative states.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse highlights the foundational principle of mind-body integration, which is the precursor to modern mindfulness and breath-work practices. It underscores the Vedic understanding that mental health and focus are deeply rooted in the regulation of the autonomous nervous system through breath control.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribed is 'Pranayama' specifically focusing on 'Kumbhaka' (breath retention) to induce 'Nishcalatva' (stillness of mind).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on 'Prana-Citta-Sambandha' (The interdependent relationship between life-force and consciousness). The bhashya explains 'Sthanutva' as the state of profound stillness where the practitioner achieves mastery (Ishatva) over internal and external fluctuations.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this reflects the 'Polyvagal theory' where slowing the breath signals safety to the autonomic nervous system, effectively moving the brain from a state of hyper-arousal (distraction) to a 'rest and digest' or meditative state, reducing anxiety and improving cognitive clarity.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Prana-tattva
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse defines life not by physical presence or consciousness alone, but by the movement of Prana (vital air). It highlights the fundamental dependency of the Jiva (individual soul) on the subtle breath within the corporeal frame.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This concept forms the cornerstone of Hatha Yoga and Ayurveda, where the health of the body is directly tied to the mastery and flow of vital breath, remaining highly relevant in modern stress-management through breathwork.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama (breath regulation), Kumbhaka (breath retention), and mindful awareness of the breath (Pranadhyana).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on Prana (Vital Energy), which is the bridge between the physical Deha (body) and the consciousness. According to Hatha Yoga Pradipika, Prana is the active force sustaining the biological functions.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a modern psychological context, this verse emphasizes the 'bottom-up' regulation of the nervous system; by controlling the breath, one influences the mind, making it a foundational tool for treating anxiety and autonomic nervous system dysregulation.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Internal Purification
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse highlights the physiological prerequisite for higher meditative states. It posits that spiritual energy cannot flow into the central channel (Sushumna) unless the subtle energy conduits are cleansed of mental and physiological 'mala' (impurities).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the psychosomatic connection where physical and mental clutter hinders the 'central' awareness, paralleling modern needs for cognitive clearing to achieve focused attention.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Hathayoga purification techniques (shatkarmas) and Pranayama for the cleansing of the nadis (nadishodhana).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Malashuddhi as a prerequisite for Sushumna-sanchara, ensuring the Prana enters the Madhyamarga.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Understood as the removal of neurological and psychological 'noise' to facilitate flow states, mirroring the yogic transition from blocked awareness to centralized consciousness.

commentary_faqs.answer: This verse addresses the prerequisite for yogic success, highlighting that physical and energetic progress is dependent on the removal of 'mala' (impurities) within the subtle body. By purifying the nadis, the practitioner prepares the internal architecture for the rise of Prana and spiritual awakening.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern terms, this relates to the physiological and psychological cleansing of the nervous system. It emphasizes that mindfulness and breathwork (Pranayama) are not merely abstract concepts but physical practices to clear blocked pathways of stress and habitual conditioning.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practices prescribed revolve around Nadi Shuddhi, specifically Pranayama and Shatkarma (cleansing techniques) to remove 'mala'.
commentary_faqs.answer: The Bhashya emphasizes Malashuddhi as the fundamental 'Hetu' (cause) for Hathasiddhi, highlighting that spiritual attainment is an organic consequence of internal energetic hygiene.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: From a secular perspective, this represents 'system reset' psychology—clearing the 'noise' or 'impurities' of trauma and emotional clutter to restore homeostasis and nervous system efficiency.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Sadhana (Spiritual Practice) and Cittashuddhi (Purification of Mind)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that mechanical practice of pranayama is insufficient; it must be coupled with a 'Sattvic' disposition. By aligning the breath with a calm and virtuous intellect, one facilitates the internal purification necessary for higher meditation.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern times, this underscores the importance of intentionality (mindfulness) in breathing exercises. It shifts the perception of breathwork from merely a physical exercise for stress relief to a holistic practice that integrates mental clarity with physiological regulation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Daily practice (nitya) of Pranayama, characterized by Satvikata (mental purity/harmony) rather than mechanical execution.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept here is Cittashuddhi (mind purification) achieved through Pranasamyama (restraint of vital airs) governed by Sattvika-buddhi (pure intellect). The commentary links the physiological act to the metaphysical result (mala-nasha).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this suggests the 'top-down' regulation of the autonomic nervous system via the intellect. It emphasizes that the efficacy of breathwork is dependent on the practitioner's mental state (set and setting).

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Pranayama
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse addresses the preparatory stage of internal cleansing through breath control. It emphasizes the balance of internal energies by specifically utilizing the lunar (Ida) channel to channelize the Prana.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the ancient understanding of neuro-respiratory regulation. In modern times, this is recognized as a somatic technique for autonomic nervous system stabilization and stress reduction.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Padmasana (posture), Pranayama (breath regulation), Puraka (inhalation through the left nostril).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around 'Nadi Shodhana' (purification of channels) via 'Ida Nadi', referred to here as 'Chandra'. The primary objective is 'Malashodhana', which involves the systematic removal of spiritual and physiological obstructions.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Breath regulation through the left nostril is often correlated with activating the parasympathetic nervous system, providing a secular, scientific mechanism for inducing a state of calm, mental focus, and physiological homeostasis.

commentary_faqs.answer: This verse addresses the physiological control of subtle energy (Prana) through breath regulation. By utilizing the 'Surya' (Pingala/Right) channel, the practitioner engages the sympathetic nervous system to increase heat and energy, gradually expanding the abdominal capacity.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This is a foundational practice in Hatha Yoga for internal purification. It underscores the ancient Indian understanding of the connection between breath, autonomic nervous system regulation, and spiritual vitality.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Kumbhaka, abdominal expansion, Nadi-sadhana.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on Prana-vayu manipulation via the Pingala-nadi, representing the heating or active aspect of the subtle body (Suksma-sarira).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern physiological studies correlate this to the regulation of vagal tone and stress management. Psychologically, it offers a method for centering consciousness and fostering somatic awareness.

commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes a specific technical methodology for Kumbhaka, emphasizing the cyclic nature of the breath. It teaches the practitioner to create a balanced circuit between exhalation and inhalation through a single side, facilitating internal steadying.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the ancient understanding of subtle body energetics, which forms the foundation of modern yogic practices focused on balancing the autonomic nervous system.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The prescribed practice is 'Puraka' (inhalation) and 'Kumbhaka' (retention) governed by strict alternating constraints (Nadi-shodhana sequence).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on 'Prana-nirodha' (restraint of vital force) within the framework of Hatha Yoga, specifically focusing on the regulation of the Vayu-marga (path of breath).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this equates to mindfulness and focused attention. In modern secular terms, it serves as a method for 'Vagal Tone' regulation, calming the sympathetic nervous system through controlled, rhythmic respiration.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Nadi Shodhana
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the fundamental practice of Nadi Shodhana pranayama, emphasizing the regulation of prana through the alternating flow of the Ida and Pingala nadis. By harmonizing the breath, the practitioner balances the internal energetic currents, leading to the purification of the subtle body.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In contemporary yoga practice, this technique is recognized as a vital tool for stress reduction, nervous system regulation, and cognitive clarity, bridging ancient energy-based physiology with modern mindfulness practices.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribes 'Puraka' (inhalation), 'Kumbhaka' (retention), and 'Rechaka' (exhalation) in an alternating rhythmic cycle to cleanse the subtle nadis.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around Nadi-shodhana (purification of channels) where the dual polarities of Chandra-nadi (Ida) and Surya-nadi (Pingala) are balanced to achieve inner equilibrium.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this practice serves as a bio-feedback mechanism to calm the autonomic nervous system, moving the practitioner from sympathetic arousal to parasympathetic restoration, thus enhancing emotional stability.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: अथ प्राणायामाभ्यासकालं तदवधिं चाह - प्रातरिति । प्रातः अरुणोदयमारभ्य सूर्योदयाद् घटिकात्रयपर्यन्ते प्रातः काले मध्यन्दिने मध्याह्ने पञ्चधा विभक्तस्य दिनस्य मध्यभागे सायं सन्ध्यात्रिणाडीप्रमितार्कास्ताद् अधस्ताद् ऊर्ध्वं चेत्युक्तलक्षणे सन्ध्याकाले रात्रेः अर्धम् अर्धरात्रः तस्मिन्नर्धरात्रे रात्रेः मध्ये मुहूर्तद्वये च शनैः अशीतिपर्यन्तं अशीतिसङ्ख्यावधि चत्रुवारं वारचतुष्टयम् । ‘कालाध्वनोरत्यन्तसंयोगे’(पा.सू.२.३.५) इति द्वितीया । चतुर्षु कालेष्वेकैकस्मिन् काले अशीतिप्राणायामाः कार्याः । अर्धरात्रे कर्तुमशक्तः चेत् त्रिसन्ध्यं कर्तव्या इति सम्प्रदायः । चतुर्वारं कृताः चेत् दिने दिने (३२०) विंशत्यधिकशतत्रयपरिमिताः प्राणायामा भवन्ति । वारत्रयं कृताः चेत् (२४०) चत्वारिंशदधिकशतत्रयपरिमिता भवन्ति ॥ ११ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Now, the author addresses the time and duration for the practice of Pranayama. 'Pratah' refers to the time starting from sunrise until three ghatikas (approx. 72 minutes) have passed. 'Madhyandina' refers to the middle part of the day. 'Sayam' refers to the twilight time, occurring before or after sunset as per standard definitions. 'Ardharatra' signifies the middle of the night, specifically the two-muhurta (96-minute) window. The instruction implies performing eighty Kumbhakas in each of these four sessions, totaling 320 breaths per day. If one is unable to perform at midnight, the tradition permits practicing at the three junctions (Trisandhya), amounting to 240 breaths.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: अब प्राणायाम के अभ्यास के काल और उसकी अवधि को बताते हैं - प्रातः। अरुणोदय से लेकर सूर्योदय के बाद तीन घटिका तक का समय प्रातःकाल है। मध्याह्न दिन के मध्य भाग को कहते हैं। सायं सन्ध्याकाल, सूर्यास्त के आसपास का समय है। अर्धरात्रि रात का मध्य भाग, दो मुहूर्तों का समय है। इन चारों कालों में अस्सी-अस्सी प्राणायाम करने चाहिए। यदि अर्धरात्रि में करने में असमर्थ हों, तो त्रिसन्ध्या (प्रातः, मध्याह्न, सायं) में करना चाहिए, यह सम्प्रदाय सम्मत नियम है। इस प्रकार करने से कुल 320 (या त्रिसन्ध्या में 240) प्राणायाम सिद्ध होते हैं।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama Krama (Sequence of Breath Control)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes the rhythmic regulation of prana (life force) by aligning practice with the natural cycles of the day. By fixing the mind through specific temporal intervals, the practitioner stabilizes the internal energy currents and facilitates mental stillness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice highlights the ancient Indian concept of bio-rhythmic synchronization, where personal spiritual discipline mirrors cosmic temporal divisions. In modern terms, this reflects a structured approach to mindfulness and stress management by creating consistent, repeatable intervals for mental focus.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice is 'Kumbhaka' (breath retention) performed 'Chatur-varam' (four times) daily, with 'Ashi-sankhya' (eighty) repetitions per session, totaling 320, or optionally 'Tri-sandhya' (three times) totaling 240.
commentary_faqs.answer: The commentary defines the 'kala' (temporal framework) for Pranayama, specifically linking it to 'Kala-adhvanoh' (the continuity of time). It establishes the 'Ashi-sankhya' (number eighty) as the quantitative requirement for 'Kumbhaka' (retention) within the 'Trisandhya' or 'Chatur-kala' framework.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern psychology recognizes the benefits of 'temporal consistency' in neurobiological conditioning. By segmenting the day into ritualized practice periods, a practitioner creates 'psychological anchors' that reduce anxiety and enhance autonomic nervous system regulation through rhythmic breath control.

sanskrit_shloka: कनीयसि भवेत् स्वेदः कम्पो भवति मध्यमे ।
text: कनीयसि भवेत् स्वेदः कम्पो भवति मध्यमे ।
transliteration: kanīyasi bhavet svedaḥ kampo bhavati madhyame .
translation: In the lowest (kanīyas) stage of Prāṇāyāma, perspiration occurs; in the intermediate (madhyama) stage, trembling (of the body) arises.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description:
कनिष्ठमध्यमोत्तमानां प्राणायामानां क्रमेण ज्ञापकविशेषानाह -
‘प्राणायामस्य मानं तु मात्राद्वादशकं स्मृतम् ।
मध्यमस्तु द्विरुद्धात्तश्चतुर्विंशतिमात्रिकः ।
मुख्यस्तु यस्त्रिरुद्धात्तः षटत्रिंशन्मात्र उच्यते ।
प्रस्वेदकम्पनोत्थानजनकश्च यथाक्रमम् ।
रोमाञ्चो ध्वनिसंवित्तिः अङ्गमोटनकम्पनम् ।
भ्रमणस्वेदजल्पाद्यं संविन्मूर्च्छा जयेद् यदा ।
घूर्णिश्चित्तान्दोलनम् ।
गोरक्षोऽपि -
‘अधमे द्वादशप्रोक्ता मध्यमे द्विगुणाः स्मृताः ।
उद्धातलक्षणं तु -
प्राणेनोत्सार्यमाणेन अपानः पीड्यते यदा ।
मात्रामाह याज्ञवल्क्यः -
‘अङ्गुष्ठाङ्गुलिमोक्षं त्रिस्त्रिर्जानुपरिमार्जनम् ।
स्कन्दपुराणे - ‘एकश्वासमयी मात्रा प्राणायामो निगद्यते’ । एतद् व्याख्यातं योगचिन्तामणौ । ‘निद्रावशंगतस्य पुंसो यावता कालेनैकःश्वासो गच्छत्यागच्छति च तावत्कालः प्राणायामस्य मात्रा इत्युच्यते’इति । अर्धश्वासाधिकद्वादशश्वासावच्छिन्नः कालः प्राणायामकालः । षड्भिः श्वासैः एकं पलं भवति । एवञ्च सार्धश्वासपलद्वयात्मकः कालः प्राणायामकालः सिद्धः । सार्धद्वादशमात्रामितः प्राणायामो यः स एवोत्तमः प्राणायाम इत्युच्यते । न च पूर्वोदाहृतलिङ्गपुराणगोरक्षवाक्यविरोधः, तत्र द्वादशमात्रकस्य प्राणायामस्याधमत्वोक्तेरिति शङ्कनीयम् ।
‘जानुं प्रदक्षिणीकुर्यान्नद्रुतं न विलम्बितम् ।
‘अङ्गुष्ठाङ्गुलिमोक्षं च जानोश्च परिमार्जनम् ।
लिङ्गपुराणगोरक्षादिवाक्येषु एकच्छोटिकावच्छिन्नस्य कालस्य मात्रात्वेन विवक्षितत्वात् । याज्ञवल्क्यादिवाक्येषु छोटिकात्रयावच्छिन्नस्य कालस्य मात्रात्वेन विवक्षणात् त्रिगुणस्य अधमस्य उत्तमत्वं तत्रापि उक्तमित्यविरोधः । सर्वेषु योगसाधनेषु प्राणायामो मुख्यः तत्सिद्धौ प्रत्याहारादीनां सिद्धेः । तदसिद्धौ प्रत्याहारादीनामसिद्धेश्च । वस्तुतस्तु प्राणायाम एव प्रत्याहारादिशब्दैर्निगद्यते । तथाचोक्तं योगचिन्तामणौ - ‘प्राणायाम एव अभ्यासक्रमेण वर्धमानः प्रत्यहारधारणाध्यानसमाधिशब्दैरुच्यते’ इति ।
तदुक्तं स्कन्दपुराणे -
प्राणायामद्विषट्केन प्रत्याहार उदाहृतः ।
भवेदीश्वरसङ्गत्यै ध्यानं द्वादशधारणम् ।
ध्यानद्वादशकेनैव समाधिरभिधीयते ।
यत्समाधौ परं ज्योतिरनन्तं स्वप्रकाशकम् ।
तथा -
‘धारणा पञ्चनाडीभिः ध्यानं स्यात् षष्टिनाडिकम् ।
गोराक्षादिभिरपि एवमेव उक्तम् । अत्रैवं व्यवस्था । किञ्चिदूनद्विचत्वारिंशद्विपलात्मकः कनिष्ठप्राणायामकालः । अयमेव एकच्छोटिकावच्छिन्नस्य मात्रात्वविवक्षया द्वादशमात्रकः कालः । किञ्चिदूनचतुरशीतिविपलात्मको मध्यमप्राणायामकालः । अयमेकच्छोटिलावच्छिन्नस्य कालस्य मात्रात्वविवक्षया षत्रिंशन्मात्रकः । पञ्चविंशत्युत्तरशतविपलात्मकः उत्तमः प्राणायामकालः । अयमेकच्छोटिकावच्छिन्नस्य कालस्य मात्रात्वविवक्षया षट्त्रिंशन्मात्रकः कालः । छोटिकात्रयाव्च्छिन्नस्य कालस्य मात्रात्वविवक्षया तु द्वादशमात्रकः एव । बन्धपूर्वकं पञ्चविंशत्युत्तरशतविपलपर्यन्तं यदा प्राणायामस्थैर्यं भवति तदा प्राणो ब्रह्मरन्ध्रं गच्छति । ब्रह्मरन्ध्रं गतः प्राणः यदा पञ्चविंशतिपलपर्यन्तं तिष्ठति तदा प्रत्याहारः । यदा पञ्चघटिकापर्यन्तं तिष्ठति तदा धारणा । यदा षष्टिघटिकापर्यन्तं तिष्ठति तदा ध्यानम् । यदा द्वादशदिनपर्यन्तं तिष्ठति तदा समाधिर्भवतीति सर्वं रमणीयम् ॥ १२ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: The text explains the distinct markers (jñāpakaviśeṣa) of Prāṇāyāma classified as kaniṣṭha, madhyama, and uttama. A Prāṇāyāma of twelve mātrās is considered lowest (adhama), twenty-four as middle (madhyama), and thirty-six as highest (uttama). These correspond to perspiration, trembling, and the rising of the prāṇa respectively. The commentary clarifies the definition of a mātrā as either the time taken for one breath or as measured by the snapping of fingers (chōṭikā), harmonizing seemingly contradictory texts by Yājñavalkya, Gorakṣa, and the Skanda Purāṇa. Ultimately, Prāṇāyāma is the root of all other stages; by perfecting it, one achieves Pratyāhāra (withdrawal), Dhāraṇā (concentration), Dhyāna (meditation), and Samādhi (absorption).
commentaries.text: The text explains the distinct markers (jñāpakaviśeṣa) of Prāṇāyāma classified as kaniṣṭha, madhyama, and uttama. A Prāṇāyāma of twelve mātrās is considered lowest (adhama), twenty-four as middle (madhyama), and thirty-six as highest (uttama). These correspond to perspiration, trembling, and the rising of the prāṇa respectively. commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Stages of Prāṇāyāma Sādhanā (Progressive physiological manifestation)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the physical signs (liṅga) accompanying the success in breath control practices. As the practitioner advances through kaniṣṭha (lowest), madhyama (middle), and uttama (highest) stages, the subtle body and physical frame respond with specific, non-pathological symptomatic changes indicating the purification of the nāḍīs.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes that spiritual progress is not merely theoretical but physiologically tangible. It serves as a diagnostic tool for practitioners to gauge their practice level while avoiding confusion between yogic symptoms and pathological ailments.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The prescribed practice is the gradual increase of 'Mātrā' (duration) of breath control, synchronized with specific bodily movements or timed snaps, leading from 'Kaniṣṭha' to 'Uttama' stages.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around the 'Jñāpakaviśeṣa' (specific indicators) of Prāṇāyāma where physical symptoms like 'Sveda' (perspiration) and 'Kampa' (trembling) signify the purification of 'Nāḍīs' (subtle channels).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this highlights the 'mind-body connection,' suggesting that meditative states are grounded in physiological regulation, providing a concrete 'bio-feedback' mechanism for modern secular meditation.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga / Deha-shuddhi
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse emphasizes the utility of sweat generated during physical practices like Pranayama. Instead of wiping it away, the yogi is advised to rub it back into the skin, believing that the vital energy (prana) contained within the sweat nourishes the body tissues.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice highlights the holistic view of the human body in Yoga, where internal secretions are seen as carriers of medicinal and energetic value, reinforcing a deeper connection with one's own physiological processes.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Sveda-mardana, Deha-shuddhi, Abhyasa.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Sveda-mardana' (rubbing of sweat), where 'Śrama-ja' (exertion-born) sweat acts as a vehicle for 'Prāṇa-shakti' absorption.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern physiological understanding of thermoregulation and the microbiome suggests that skin absorption and friction can stimulate blood flow, while the psychological aspect involves a mindful acceptance of bodily products as extensions of one's own energy, countering modern detachment from the physical self.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Mitahara (Measured Diet in Yoga)
commentary_faqs.answer: In the path of Yoga, the regulation of diet is essential for balancing the nervous system and physical health. The consumption of 'sattvic' substances like milk and ghee provides the necessary nourishment for the subtle body to undergo intense practices without depleting vital energies.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This underscores the connection between physical nutrition and mental state; in modern times, it highlights the importance of gut health and anti-inflammatory diets in managing stress and mental stability.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Mitahara (regulated diet), specific intake of milk (kṣīra) and clarified butter (ājya) to facilitate Kevala Kumbhaka.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is Mitahara, specifically the application of Sattvic dietary restrictions to stabilize the Pranic flow (Prana-sthirata) during initial sadhana stages.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Focuses on 'neuro-nutrition' where specific caloric intake is utilized to support sustained cognitive performance and biological homeostasis during demanding physical or psychological training.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Gradual Self-Mastery (Abhyāsa and Vairāgya)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse employs a metaphor of taming wild animals to illustrate the necessity of gradual, patient control over one's vital energy (Prana) and mind. Sudden or forceful attempts at self-regulation are depicted as counterproductive or dangerous, advocating instead for a steady, incremental process.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This principle is foundational to Hatha Yoga and modern behavioral psychology. It suggests that deep-seated habits or physiological patterns are not overcome by brute willpower alone, but through consistent, gentle practice (sādhana) over time.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice prescribed is Sanaih-sanaih-abhyasa (gradual, repetitive practice) and avoidance of Sahasa (abrupt/hasty effort).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is Prana-nirodha (control of vital breath) through the principle of Krama (gradual progression) to avoid Hatha (forceful) exhaustion of the nervous system.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern terms, this reflects the neuroplasticity principle where cognitive and emotional regulation requires a long-term, incremental approach to reprogram neural pathways rather than impulsive, high-intensity interventions.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Prana-vidya and Yogic Physiology
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse emphasizes that the rhythmic control of breath (prāṇāyāma) is not merely a physical exercise but a restorative technique to clear obstructions (nāḍī-śodhana) in the subtle body. By harmonizing the life force, the practitioner eradicates the root causes of imbalance that manifest as physical and mental disease.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern context, this aligns with scientific studies on the autonomic nervous system and the benefits of deep breathing for stress reduction, blood pressure regulation, and immune system optimization.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practices: Yukta-prāṇāyāma (regulated breath-work), disciplined daily repetition, and balanced application (yukti).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on Prāṇāyāma as a Prāṇa-saṃyama process where the regulation of the vital air leads to 'roga-kṣaya' (dissolution of disease).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern psychological relevance: Correlates to neuro-feedback and vagal tone modulation which aids in psychosomatic healing and resilience against chronic stress.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Dosha-samyata (Balance of Bio-energies)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse warns of the physiological consequences of improper Pranayamic practice, where the vital air (Vayu) becomes agitated rather than refined. It emphasizes that yoga is not merely an external exercise but requires precise control to avoid aggravating the body's internal systems (Doshas).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern context, this serves as a cautionary principle against 'fast-track' or unregulated yoga practice. It highlights the necessity of expert guidance, as psychophysical techniques can have adverse somatic effects if performed contrary to classical instruction.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice is Yukta-pranayama (regulated breathing) guided by a Guru to avoid Prana-doshotpadana.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept here is Pranavayu-vikriti resulting from improper control, leading to systemic imbalance of Vata-dosha.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Reflects the importance of 'mindful progression' and physiological safety in modern therapeutic yoga, warning against over-exertion or incorrect breath-retention techniques that may trigger stress-induced psychosomatic symptoms.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Since various diseases arise from the disturbance of the wind (prana), the text says 'yuktam yuktam'. One should exhale the air (prana) in a balanced way, meaning during the process of exhalation, one should release it slowly and gradually, not with force. Likewise, one should inhale (purayet) in a balanced way, neither too little nor too much. Furthermore, one should engage the locks like Jalandhara Bandha as appropriate. By practicing in this manner, one attains accomplishment, specifically Hatha Siddhi.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama (Regulation of Vital Breath)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes the principle of moderation in yogic breathing practices, stating that breath control is not about forceful exertion but about rhythmic, balanced regulation. Excess or deficiency in the practice of Rechaka (exhalation) and Puraka (inhalation) can lead to physiological imbalance, hence the repetition of 'yuktam' (balanced/appropriate).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse is a cornerstone of Hatha Yoga, advocating for an incremental and systematic approach to wellness, applicable today in stress management and mindfulness techniques where controlled breathing acts as a regulator for the nervous system.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice involves Gradual Exhalation (Rechaka), Regulated Inhalation (Puraka), and the integration of Bandhas (Jalandhara Bandha).
commentary_faqs.answer: Prana-samyamana and the prevention of Vata-dosha through proper regulation (Yukta-krama) of Rechaka and Puraka.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this acts as a vagal-toning exercise, reducing 'fight or flight' stress responses by ensuring the autonomic nervous system is not over-stimulated through erratic breathing patterns.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Nadi Shuddhi (Purification of the Subtle Channels)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse addresses the physiological and subtle impact of pranayama, emphasizing that internal purity manifests in tangible physical indicators. It posits that the practitioner does not simply guess their progress but experiences objective signs of purification.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern yoga, this concept translates to the objective measurement of somatic health and mental equilibrium resulting from respiratory regulation, bridging the gap between esoteric practice and observable well-being.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice specifically highlighted is Yukta-pranayama, implying rhythmic and regulated breathing aligned with classical pedagogical standards.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on Prana-kriya whereby Nadi-shuddhi marks the state of internal coherence of the subtle body, moving from internal purification (antaranga) to manifest external physical health (bahya-lakshana).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this refers to the 'somatic-feedback loop' where regular mindful breathing patterns decrease sympathetic nervous system arousal, manifesting as measurable physiological calm and improved physical vitality.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: मेदाद्याधिक्ये उपायान्तरमाह - मेदश्लेष्माधिक इति । मेदश्च श्लेष्मा च मेदश्लेष्माणौ तावधिकौ यस्य स तादृशः पुरुषः । पूर्वं प्राणायामाभ्यासात् प्राङ् न तु प्राणायामाभ्यासकाले षट् कर्माणि वक्ष्यमाणानि समाचरेत् सम्यगाचरेत् । अन्यस्तु मेदश्लेष्माधिक्यरहितस्तु तानि षट्कर्माणि नाचरेत् । तत्र हेतुमाह । दोषाणां वातपित्तकफानां समस्य भावः समभावः समत्वं तस्माद् दोषाणां समत्वादित्यर्थः ॥ २१ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Addressing the excess of Medas and others, the author speaks of another method: 'medaśleṣmādhikaḥ'. One whose excess of Medas and Śleṣman is prevalent. Before the practice of Prāṇāyāma, and not during the practice of Prāṇāyāma, one should properly perform the six actions (ṣaṭkarmāṇi) which will be mentioned. Others, who do not have an excess of Medas and Śleṣman, should not perform these six actions. He gives the reason for this: 'dosāṇām'—the state of balance of the dosas, namely Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha, is 'samabhāva' or 'samatvam'; therefore, one performs this for the sake of the balance of the dosas.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Śodhana-kriyā (Purification Practices)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse establishes that internal physical purification is a prerequisite for advanced yoga practices like Prāṇāyāma for those whose systems are imbalanced by excess Kapha and Medas. It emphasizes that yoga is not one-size-fits-all, but requires individual assessment of bodily constituents (Dosas).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the Ayurvedic principle that health is the foundation for spiritual practice; a congested body hinders the flow of Prāṇa, necessitating physical detox before subtle breath-work.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice is restricted to Ṣaṭkarman (Dhauti, Basti, Neti, Nauli, Trāṭaka, Kapālabhāti) specifically for those with Vāta/Kapha imbalance.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Doṣa-samatva (homeostasis of bio-energies) as a prerequisite for Sādhana, emphasizing that internal purity (Śuddhi) via the six Kriyās is essential for the efficacy of Prāṇāyāma.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Reflects a bio-individualized approach to health; emphasizes that psychological or meditative progress is stunted if one ignores the physiological baseline or systemic toxicity (metabolic excess).

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Shatkarma (Purification Techniques)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse introduces the essential cleansing processes of Hatha Yoga designed to remove physical and energetic impurities (mala) from the body. These internal purifications are considered prerequisites for the successful practice of Asana and Pranayama.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These practices remain highly relevant in modern integrative health, serving as traditional methods for maintaining internal organ hygiene, improving focus, and achieving physical resilience.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Dhauti, Vasti, Neti, Trataka, Nauli (and Kapalbhati which is implied in the full Shatkarma set).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on 'Shatkarma' (six actions of purification), which are foundational for 'deha-shuddhi' (purification of the body) to prepare the 'nadi' channels for 'prana' flow.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: These techniques offer a psycho-somatic approach to health, emphasizing the relationship between organ cleansing (detoxification) and clarity of mind, which aligns with modern holistic wellness paradigms.

commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the therapeutic efficacy of Dhauti-karma (cleansing technique) in Hatha Yoga. It highlights the physiological restoration brought about by cleansing the internal systems, specifically targeting imbalances in the Kapha dosha.

commentary_faqs.answer: Modern relevance lies in detoxification strategies. Psychologically, removing physical 'mala' (impurities) is linked to reducing 'tamas' or lethargy, improving respiratory function and metabolic health in sedentary lifestyles.

अथ वस्तिकर्माह -
तदनन्तरं भोजने विलम्बोऽपि न कार्यः । केचित्तु पूर्वं मूलाधारेण वायोराकर्षणमभ्यस्य जले स्थित्वा पायौ नालप्रवेशमन्तरेणैव वस्तिकर्माभ्यस्यन्ति । तथ करणे सर्वं जलं बहिर्नायाति ।
अतो नानारोगधातुक्षयादिसम्भवाच्च तथा वस्तिकर्म नैव विधेयम् । किमन्यथा स्वात्मारामः पायौ न्यस्तनालः इति ब्रूयात् ॥ २६ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Now, he describes the Vasti-karma. After that, one should not delay in eating. Some practitioners practice the attraction of Vayu (prana) via the Muladhara, and while standing in water, they perform the Vasti-karma without inserting a tube into the anus. However, by doing so, not all the water is expelled. Therefore, due to the risk of various diseases and the depletion of bodily elements (dhatukshaya), such a method of Vasti-karma should not be practiced. Otherwise, why would the author (Svatmarama) say 'with a tube inserted into the anus'?

commentary_faqs.answer: Modern wellness recognizes this as an ancient precursor to irrigation therapy, emphasizing the connection between physical internal hygiene and psychological clarity.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice: Vasti-karma performed with a tube (Nala) as specified in the authoritative texts, combined with careful dietary management.
commentary_faqs.answer: The commentary highlights the importance of 'Vidhi' (procedural correctness) in 'Shodhana' (purification), warning against 'Dhatukshaya' (depletion of bodily tissues) caused by improper 'Abhyasa'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: The text serves as a psychological caution against shortcutting rigorous protocols; it emphasizes that incomplete or incorrect execution of complex disciplines leads to systemic imbalance rather than health.

commentaries.description:
अथ नेतिकर्माह -
यावता सूत्रेण सम्यक् नेतिकर्मभवेत् तावद् ग्राह्यम् । नासा नासिका सैव नालः सच्छिद्रत्वात् तस्मिन् प्रवेशयेत् । मुखान्निर्गमयेत् निष्कसयेत् । तत्प्रकारस्त्वेवम् । सूत्रप्रान्तं नासानाले प्रवेश्य इतरनासापुटमङ्गुल्या निरुध्य पूरकं कुर्यात् । पुनश्च मुखेन रेचयेत् । पुनः पुनः एवं कुर्वतः मुखे सूत्रप्रान्तमायाति । तत्सूत्रप्रान्तं नासाबहिस्थसूत्रप्रान्तं च गृहीत्वा शनैः चालयेदिति । चकारदेकस्मिन् नासानाले प्रवेश्य इतरस्मिन् निर्गमयेदित्युक्तम् । तत्प्रकारस्तु एकस्मिन् नासानाले सूत्रप्रान्तं प्रवेश्य इतरनासापुटमङ्गुल्या निरुध्य पूरकं कुर्यात् पश्चादितरनासानालेन रेचयेत् । पुनः पुनरेवं कुर्वतः इतरनासानाले सूत्रप्रान्तमायाति तस्य पूर्ववच्चालनं कुर्यादिति । अयं प्रकारस्तु बहुवारं कुर्वतः कदाचित् भवति । एषोक्ता सिद्धैः अणिमादिगुणसम्पन्नैः । तदुक्तम् - अवाप्ताष्टगुणैश्वर्याःसिद्धाः सद्भिः निरूपिताः । नेतिः निगद्यते नेतिरिति कथ्यते ॥ २९ ॥
commentaries.text:
अथ नेतिकर्माह -
यावता सूत्रेण सम्यक् नेतिकर्मभवेत् तावद् ग्राह्यम् । नासा नासिका सैव नालः सच्छिद्रत्वात् तस्मिन् प्रवेशयेत् । मुखान्निर्गमयेत् निष्कसयेत् । तत्प्रकारस्त्वेवम् । सूत्रप्रान्तं नासानाले प्रवेश्य इतरनासापुटमङ्गुल्या निरुध्य पूरकं कुर्यात् । पुनश्च मुखेन रेचयेत् । पुनः पुनः एवं कुर्वतः मुखे सूत्रप्रान्तमायाति । तत्सूत्रप्रान्तं नासाबहिस्थसूत्रप्रान्तं च गृहीत्वा शनैः चालयेदिति । चकारदेकस्मिन् नासानाले प्रवेश्य इतरस्मिन् निर्गमयेदित्युक्तम् । तत्प्रकारस्तु एकस्मिन् नासानाले सूत्रप्रान्तं प्रवेश्य इतरनासापुटमङ्गुल्या निरुध्य पूरकं कुर्यात् पश्चादितरनासानालेन रेचयेत् । पुनः पुनरेवं कुर्वतः इतरनासानाले सूत्रप्रान्तमायाति तस्य पूर्ववच्चालनं कुर्यादिति । अयं प्रकारस्तु बहुवारं कुर्वतः कदाचित् भवति । एषोक्ता सिद्धैः अणिमादिगुणसम्पन्नैः । तदुक्तम् - अवाप्ताष्टगुणैश्वर्याःसिद्धाः सद्भिः निरूपिताः । नेतिः निगद्यते नेतिरिति कथ्यते ॥ २९ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Now the Neti technique is described: One should take a thread of the appropriate length that allows for effective Neti performance. 'Nasa' refers to the nostrils; because it is hollow, one should insert the thread there and draw it out through the mouth. The process is thus: insert the end of the thread into the nostril, block the other nostril with a finger, and perform inhalation. Then exhale through the mouth. Repeating this repeatedly, the thread will emerge from the mouth. Then, holding both ends of the thread—the one outside the nose and the one outside the mouth—one should move it slowly. The word 'ca' (in the original text) implies the method of inserting in one nostril and drawing it out through the other: insert the thread end into one nostril, close the other with a finger, inhale, then exhale through the other nostril. Doing this repeatedly, the thread emerges from the other nostril, and one should move it as before. This method occurs sometimes after many attempts. This has been spoken by the Siddhas, who are endowed with qualities like Anima (subtlety). As it is said: those who have attained the eightfold divine attributes are described by the wise as Siddhas. This is called Neti.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: अब नेतिकर्म का वर्णन है - जिस लंबाई का सूत्र नेतिकर्म के लिए उपयुक्त हो, उसे ग्रहण करें। नासिका छिद्रयुक्त होती है, उसमें सूत्र प्रविष्ट कराएं और मुख से बाहर निकालें। इसका प्रकार यह है: सूत्र के एक सिरे को नासिका में डालकर, दूसरी नासिका को अंगुली से बंद कर पूरक (श्वास अंदर लेना) करें। पुनः मुख से रेचन करें। बार-बार ऐसा करने पर सूत्र का सिरा मुख में आ जाता है। तब बाहर निकले हुए और नासिका के बाहर स्थित सिरे को पकड़कर धीरे-धीरे चलाएं। 'चकार' से यह कहा गया है कि एक नासिका में प्रवेश कराकर दूसरी से निकालें। उसका प्रकार यह है कि एक नासिका में सूत्र डालकर दूसरी को बंद करें, पूरक करें और फिर दूसरी नासिका से रेचन करें। बार-बार करने पर सूत्र दूसरी नासिका से बाहर आ जाता है। यह विधि सिद्धि प्राप्त महापुरुषों द्वारा कही गई है, जिन्हें अणिमा आदि आठ सिद्धियाँ प्राप्त हैं।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Shodhana (Purification)
commentary_faqs.answer: Neti is one of the six cleansing processes (Shatkarmas) in Hatha Yoga designed to purify the nasal passages. By removing physical obstructions, it prepares the practitioner for deeper breathing (Pranayama) and spiritual focus.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Practiced historically for physical health and clarity of the mind, it remains highly relevant today as a therapeutic practice for respiratory health, sinusitis, and stress reduction through breath regulation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Sutraneti (Thread Neti), Nasal irrigation, regulation of Prana through controlled inhalation (Puraka) and exhalation (Rechaka).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Shodhana' (Purification) involving the Srotas (channels) and the vital role of the Siddhas in preserving the tradition of Kriya Yoga and Shatkarma.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychosomatically, the nasal cleansing influences the autonomic nervous system. It is used as a functional tool for physiological homeostasis, reducing allergies and enhancing focus through the unobstructed flow of breath.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga / Shatkarma (Kriya)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse refers to the physiological and subtle spiritual benefits of Neti (nasal cleansing). By purifying the cranial region (kapāla), the practitioner removes blockages that inhibit higher perception (divyadṛṣṭi).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the mind-body connection in Indian medicine and yoga, suggesting that physical purity is the precursor to meditative depth.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Jala Neti or Sutra Neti as a foundational Shatkarma technique for kriya-yoga practitioners.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Kapala-shodhana' pertains to the purification of the frontal sinuses and the subtle 'kapala' region, facilitating the awakening of 'divya-drishti' or the inner intuitive faculty.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern psychological interpretations suggest that physiological cleansing of the respiratory pathways significantly reduces cognitive interference, leading to enhanced focus and clarity (mindfulness).

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Dharana (Concentration)
commentary_faqs.answer: Trataka is a foundational yogic technique involving steady, unblinking focus on a singular point. It serves to pacify the restless mind (citta-vritti) and enhance internal clarity by integrating ocular focus with mental stability.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern era of screen-dependency and digital distraction, Trataka is highly relevant as a visual hygiene practice that combats eye strain while fostering sustained attention span and emotional regulation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Fixed gazing, concentration, reduction of eye-blink rate, mental poise.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Trataka involves 'Ekagrata' (one-pointedness) of the mind through visual fixation, serving as an intermediate stage between external object focus and 'Antardhyana' (internal meditation).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Secularly, this acts as a 'mindfulness anchor'. Psychologically, it mitigates cognitive fragmentation by training the brain to inhibit peripheral stimuli, providing a template for focus in high-stress environments.

commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the therapeutic efficacy of Trataka (fixed-gazing meditation). It suggests that the practice not only heals ocular disorders but also serves as a sensory 'gatekeeper' against tamasic qualities like lethargy.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Trataka is widely practiced today as a technique for improving concentration (dharana) and mental clarity, proving its longevity as a physiological and psychological tool.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Trataka (Fixed gazing), Dristi-sadhana, sensory withdrawal.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on 'Trataka' as a 'Cakshurbhushana' and 'Tamoguna-nirodhaka' tool, acting as a functional barrier against physical and cognitive inertia.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Clinically, it aids in improving ocular focus and reducing screen-induced fatigue. Psychologically, it functions as an attention-training exercise to overcome cognitive lethargy and executive dysfunction.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Shatkarma
commentary_faqs.answer: Nauli is a primary cleansing technique (Shatkarma) in Hatha Yoga involving the isolation and churning of the rectus abdominis muscles. It is designed to stimulate the digestive fire (Jatharagni) and cleanse the abdominal organs, facilitating physical and energetic purification.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Nauli remains a cornerstone of traditional yoga practice globally, recognized for its profound benefits in improving metabolic function and strengthening the core. It serves as a bridge between physical conditioning and the subtle energetic manipulation required for higher states of consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice involves 'Uddiyana Bandha' as a prerequisite, followed by 'Madhyama-nauli' (central isolation) and 'Vama-dakshina-nauli' (side isolation).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on 'Jatharagni-diipana' (kindling the digestive fire) through mechanical manipulation of the visceral region, which is fundamental to 'Kaya-shuddhi' (purification of the body).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern relevance lies in visceral massage and digestive health regulation, helping to counter sedentary lifestyle-induced metabolic disorders through targeted abdominal muscle contraction.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Ayurvedic Physiology and Hathayoga
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse emphasizes the role of yogic practices, specifically Nauli, in restoring Agni (metabolic fire). By ensuring proper digestion and metabolism, the practitioner achieves physical health, which manifests as mental clarity and bliss (ananda).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern life, where digestive disorders and stress are prevalent, this highlights the link between internal physical regulation and mental happiness, proving that physiological health is a prerequisite for higher states of consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Nauli-kriya, Agni-dipana, Pachan-sadhana.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept addresses 'Jatharagni-sandipana' (kindling of metabolic fire) as the foundational element of 'Deha-shuddhi' (purification of the body).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Refers to the psychosomatic connection where the 'gut-brain axis' is addressed; a healthy digestive system leads to emotional stability and the reduction of physiological anxiety.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Shatkarma (Yogic Purification)
commentary_faqs.answer: Kapalabhati is a foundational Shatkarma aimed at clearing the nadis (subtle energy channels) and refining the consciousness. It functions by creating rapid, rhythmic abdominal movements to purge toxins and stagnant prana.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern era, Kapalabhati is widely used as a respiratory exercise to improve lung capacity, alleviate stress, and sharpen mental clarity.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed as a rhythmic 'rechakā' (exhalation) and 'purakā' (inhalation) exercise focus, specifically emphasizing forceful expulsion of breath.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Kapalabhati centers on 'śodhana' (purification) of the 'kapāla' (frontal lobe/skull) to achieve 'bhāti' (effulgence or luminosity). It is considered a preparatory 'kriyā' to balance the 'prāṇa-vāya'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, the practice acts as a neuro-stimulant that reduces 'tamas' (lethargy) and modulates the autonomic nervous system, effectively acting as a somatic intervention for anxiety and mental fatigue.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Shatkarma (Yogic Purification)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse underscores the necessity of physical purification before advanced yoga practice. By removing 'mala' (impurities) and 'kapha' (phlegm), the practitioner achieves a lightness of body that facilitates higher states of concentration.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern times, this emphasizes the mind-body connection, suggesting that psychological clarity is often obstructed by physiological stagnation or 'toxins' that must be addressed through lifestyle and purification.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Dhauti, Basti, Neti, Trataka, Nauli, Kapalbhati (The Shatkarmas).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on 'śodhana' (purification) as a prerequisite for 'prāṇāyāma' (breath regulation), ensuring the 'nāḍīs' are free from 'doṣa' and 'mala'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Addresses the 'leaky gut' and 'metabolic syndrome' phenomena through ancient detox protocols, offering a somatic approach to mental hygiene.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Suddhi (Purification) through Prana
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse asserts that Pranayama functions as the primary catalyst for cleansing the subtle body of 'malas' or obstructions. By regulating the vital breath, the practitioner dries up the accumulated psychological and physiological residues that hinder higher states of consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This emphasizes the priority of breath-work over complex physical cleansing rituals (Shatkarmas) in specific yogic lineages, highlighting a shift from external hygiene to internal energetic refinement, which is highly relevant in modern stress-reduction techniques.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Regular practice of Pranayama as a sufficient means for internal detoxification, thereby making elaborate Shatkarmas secondary or optional.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around the primacy of Prana-shuddhi over external purification, where 'mala' represents the obstacles in the Nadis, and 'Acharya' serves as the bridge between theoretical knowledge and practical conduct.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this validates the 'bottom-up' approach where physical breath regulation influences the nervous system to purge anxiety and mental noise, mirroring modern biofeedback and vagus nerve stimulation techniques.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Kriya (Cleansing Technique)
commentary_faqs.answer: Gajakarani refers to a specific yogic practice aimed at cleansing the digestive system and esophagus by inducing voluntary emesis. It symbolizes the yogic mastery over bodily functions and the purification of the subtle channels (nadis).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern times, it is recognized as a profound physiological cleansing process. It bridges the gap between ancient somatic control and contemporary psychosomatic health management.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice: 'Vamana' (voluntary emesis) performed with focused intention to clear the 'Jathara' (stomach).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Gajakarani' signifies the 'Shodhana' (purification) of the 'Koshas', specifically targeting the 'Annamaya Kosha' by neutralizing 'Pitta' (bile) excess.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern psychological relevance lies in the mind-body feedback loop; the ability to consciously regulate autonomic physiological processes empowers the practitioner to gain psychological self-regulation and emotional resilience.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama as Universal Discipline
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse establishes that Pranayama is not merely a human endeavor but a divine necessity. Even exalted beings like Brahma must engage in the rhythmic control of Vayu (prana) to maintain their status and cosmic function.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the hierarchy of yogic discipline, suggesting that if divine entities require breath regulation, then mortal beings are absolutely dependent upon it for spiritual evolution and psychological balance.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama (Breath Control), Abhyasa (Consistent Practice), Nityata (Regularity).
commentary_faqs.answer: The bhashya emphasizes the 'Prana-sadhana' as a path to divinity; it posits that Vayu (breath) represents the subtle energy (Prana) that supports both cosmic and individual existence (Sthiti).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Breath regulation is recognized in modern psychology as a primary tool for autonomic nervous system modulation, managing stress, and enhancing cognitive focus by influencing the Vagal tone.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Chitta-vritti-nirodha
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse establishes that the mastery over prana (breath) and the stabilization of the mind are the twin pillars of yogic liberation. When breath is regulated and consciousness remains free from agitation, the individual transcends the cyclical limitations of temporal existence and karmic causality.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This concept is foundational to Hatha Yoga and Raja Yoga, suggesting that physiological control directly impacts psychological clarity, a principle heavily validated in modern neuro-feedback and mindfulness practices.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama (breath regulation) and Citta-vritti-nirodha (cessation of mental fluctuations).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept addresses the state of 'Jivanmukti' where 'Prana' and 'Citta' are synchronized, leading to 'Kala-atita' (beyond time) and 'Karma-vimukti' (liberation from action).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the physiological-psychological feedback loop: a steady breath creates a steady mind, which in turn reduces stress-related aging (Time/Kala) and reactionary behavioral patterns (Karma).

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Nadi Shodhana (Purification of the Subtle Channels)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that spiritual progress in Yoga is predicated on the physiological and subtle purification of the nadi-chakra. By regulating the vital life force (prana), the practitioner clears the blockages that hinder the upward movement of energy.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern terms, this corresponds to nervous system regulation and the stabilization of autonomic functions through rhythmic breathing, which serves as a foundation for psychological clarity and meditation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Asana, Jalandhara Bandha, and the systematic cultivation of breath control to achieve physiological stillness.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around Nadi-Shuddhi (purification of subtle channels) as a precursor to Prana-Pravesha (entry of vital air) into the Sushumna Nadi, which is the gateway to higher states of consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice acts as a tool for neuro-respiratory synchronization, helping individuals manage stress and chronic emotional turbulence by recalibrating the autonomic nervous system.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: मारुत इति । मध्ये सुषुम्नामध्ये सञ्चारः सम्यक् चरणं गमनं मूर्धपर्यन्तं यस्य सः मध्यसञ्चारः तस्मिन् सति मनसः स्थैर्यं ध्येयाकारवृत्तिप्रवाहः जायते प्रादुर्भवति । यो मनसः सुस्थिरीभावः सुष्ठुस्थिरीभवनं सैव मनोन्मन्यवस्था । मनोन्मनीशब्दः उन्मनीपर्यायः । तथाग्रे वक्ष्यति - ‘राजयोगः समाधिश्च’ । (४.३) इत्यादिना ॥ ४२ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Regarding 'Marute' (the breath): When the movement, the proper flow (sañcāra) of the breath into the 'middle'—the Sushumna—reaches the head, this state is called Madhyasañcāra. When this happens, the 'Sthairya' (stillness) of the mind—the flow of consciousness taking the form of the object of meditation—arises or manifests. That which is the 'Susthiribhava' (state of being well-established) of the mind is known as the 'Manonmanyavastha' (the state of mind-transcendence). The word 'Manonmani' is a synonym for 'Unmani' (the state beyond the mind). It will be mentioned further [in the text] such as 'Rajayoga and Samadhi' (4.3).

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Manonmani (Mind-transcendence)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse establishes a causal link between breath regulation and mental stillness. By directing the prana into the Sushumna Nadi, the practitioner transcends the fluctuations of the mind, leading to the state of Unmani.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This emphasizes the psychophysical connection in Yoga, where physiological control (prana) serves as the anchor for cognitive stillness, a concept mirrored in modern mindfulness practices.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The primary practice is Kumbhaka or Pranayama aimed at Sushumna-gati, specifically concentrating on directing the breath through the central nadi to induce Samadhi.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept explores Prana-Sanchara (movement of breath) as the gateway to Manonmani, where the Chitta-vritti (fluctuations of the mind) cease and the practitioner reaches an Unmani (thoughtless) state.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This provides a somatic approach to mental health; just as modern psychology recognizes the role of the parasympathetic nervous system in calming anxiety, this verse offers the physiological mechanism of breath control to achieve psychological equilibrium.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Sadhana and Vicitra Kumbhaka
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that the path to higher yogic realization requires a systematic application of varied breath control techniques. These practices are not mere physical exercises but precise methodologies designed to cultivate specific internal states conducive to higher consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern era, this highlights the necessity of expert guidance (Vidhanajna) in practice, cautioning against 'one-size-fits-all' approaches to mindfulness and breathwork, emphasizing individual suitability.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice is 'Kumbhaka' (breath retention) performed with knowledge of 'Vidhana' (systematic procedure), supported by 'Pratyahara' (sensory withdrawal).
commentary_faqs.answer: The Bhashya explores 'Siddhi' as an outcome of 'Vicitra Kumbhaka', framed within the broader Yogic methodology (Vidhana) which integrates Pratyahara and traditional stages.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this suggests that emotional and cognitive regulation ('Siddhi') is not instantaneous but requires structured, progressive training (Abhyasa) rather than impulsive techniques.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama / Hatha Yoga
commentary_faqs.answer: Kumbhaka refers to the cessation or retention of breath, a fundamental pillar of Hatha Yoga practice for mastering Prana. It signifies the transition from external respiratory movement to internal energetic control.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern times, this relates to techniques for nervous system regulation and stress reduction, emphasizing the link between breath, mind, and emotional stability.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Abhyasa (consistent practice) of specific breathing patterns; focus on 'Kumbhaka' (suspension) and 'Nama-nirdesha' (classification of techniques).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Ashtakumbhaka' (eight varieties of breath retention), which are instrumental in 'Prana-nirodha' (restraint of vital energy) as a prerequisite for 'Samadhi'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this offers a structured method for 'vagus nerve stimulation' and autonomic nervous system management, providing a secular framework for emotional resilience and mental stillness.

commentaries.description:
अथ हठसिद्धौ अनन्यसिद्धां पारमहंसीं सर्वकुम्भकसाधारणयुक्तिमाह त्रिभिः पूरकान्त इति ।
जालन्धर इत्यभिधा नाम यस्य स जालन्धराभिधो बन्धः, बध्नाति प्राणवायुमिति बन्धः । कण्ठाकुञ्चनपूर्वकं चिबुकस्य हृदि स्थापनं जालन्धरबन्धः पूरकान्ते पूरकस्य अन्ते पूरकानन्तरं झटिति कर्तव्यः । तुशब्दात् कुम्भकादौ । उड्डियानकस्तु कुम्भकान्ते कुम्भकस्यान्ते किञ्चित् कुम्भकशेषे रेचकस्यादौ रेचकादौ रेचकात् पूर्वं कर्तव्यः । प्रयत्नविशेषेण नाभिप्रदेशस्य पृष्ठतः आकर्षणमुड्डियानबन्धः ॥ ४५ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: Now, to attain Hatha-Siddhi, the author explains the unique Parama-hamsa technique applicable to all Kumbhaka (retention) practices in three verses, beginning with 'Purakante'. The lock named Jalandhara is so called because it 'binds' (badhnati) the Prana-vayu. Jalandhara Bandha involves the contraction of the throat and the placement of the chin against the chest; it must be performed immediately after the Puraka (inhalation). The word 'tu' implies it may also be performed at the beginning of Kumbhaka. Uddiyana Bandha is to be performed at the end of Kumbhaka, when only a little retention remains, just before the Rechaka (exhalation). Uddiyana Bandha is defined as the contraction and drawing of the navel region towards the spine through special effort.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: अब हठसिद्धि के लिए, लेखक अनन्यसिद्ध पारमहंसी युक्ति को समझा रहे हैं जो सभी कुंभकों में सामान्य है। जालंधर नामक बंध उसे कहते हैं जो प्राणवायु को बांधता है। कंठ का संकुचन करके चिबुक (ठुड्डी) को हृदय (छाती) के पास स्थापित करना जालंधर बंध है, जिसे पूरक के अंत में तत्काल करना चाहिए। 'तु' शब्द से संकेत है कि यह कुंभक के आरंभ में भी किया जा सकता है। उड्डियान बंध कुंभक के अंत में, जब थोड़ा कुंभक शेष रहे और रेचक से पहले करना चाहिए। प्रयत्न विशेष से नाभि प्रदेश को पीठ की ओर खींचना ही उड्डियान बंध है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Pranayama Techniques
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse introduces the Jalandhara Bandha, a vital energetic seal in yogic practice. It serves to redirect and contain the prana (vital life force) after inhalation to facilitate deeper meditative states.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These bandhas are the foundation of physiological regulation in yoga, promoting autonomic nervous system balance and focusing mental energy during modern mindfulness practices.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Puraka (inhalation), Kumbhaka (retention), Jalandhara Bandha (throat lock), Uddiyana Bandha (abdominal lock).
commentary_faqs.answer: The mechanism of 'Bandha' acts as a 'khecari' precursor, regulating 'prana-vayu' via 'kantha-akuncana' (throat contraction) and 'cibuka-sthapana' (chin placement) to achieve 'hatha-siddhi'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychosomatic regulation of the vagus nerve and diaphragmatic control to reduce anxiety and increase physiological resilience.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description: अधस्तादिति । कण्ठस्य सङ्कोचनं कण्ठसङ्कोचनं तस्मिन् कृते सति जालन्धरबन्धे कृते सति इत्यर्थः । आश्वव्यवहितोत्तरमेव अधस्तात् अधः प्रदेशात् आकुञ्चनेन आधाराकुञ्चनेन मूलबन्धेन इत्यर्थः । मध्ये नाभिप्रदेशे पश्चिमतः पृष्ठतः तानं ताननम् आकर्षणं तेन उड्डियानबन्धेन इत्यर्थः । उक्तरीत्या कृतेन बन्धत्रयेण प्राणो वायुः ब्रह्मनाडीं सुषुम्नां गच्छतीति ब्रह्मनाडिगः सुषुम्नानाडिगामी स्यात् इत्यर्थः । अत्रेदं रहस्यम् । यदि श्रीगुरुमुखात् जिह्वाबन्धः सम्यक् परिज्ञातः तर्हि जिह्वाबन्धपूर्वकेन जालन्धरबन्धेनैव प्राणायामः सिध्यति । वायुप्रकोपो नैव भवति । ‘वपुःक़ृशत्वं वदने प्रसन्नता’ (२.७८) इत्यादीनि सर्वाणि लक्षणानि जायन्त इति मूलबन्धोड्डियानबन्धौ नोपयुक्तौ । तयोः जिह्वाबन्धपूर्वकेण जालन्धरबन्धेन अन्यथासिद्धत्वात् । जिह्वाबन्धो न विदितश्चेत् ‘अधस्तात् कुञ्चनेन’ इति श्लोकोक्तरीत्या प्राणायामाः कर्तव्याः । त्रयोऽपि बन्धाः गुरुमुखाद् ज्ञातव्याः । मूलबन्धस्तु सम्यक् अज्ञातः नानारोगोत्पादकः । तथा हि, यदि मूलबन्धे कृते धातुक्षयो विष्टम्भोऽग्निमान्द्यं नादमान्द्यं गुटिकासमूहाकारम् अजस्येव पुरीषं स्यात् तदा मूलबन्धः सम्यक् न ज्ञातः इति बोध्यम् । यदि तु धातुपुष्टिः सम्यक् मलशुद्धिः अग्निदीप्तिः सम्यक् नादाभिव्यक्तिश्च स्यात् तदा ज्ञेयं मूलबन्धः सम्यक् ज्ञात इति ॥ ४६ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: The commentary explains that 'kanthasankochane' signifies the Jalandhara Bandha. 'Adhastat kuncanena' refers to the Mula Bandha (contraction of the base). By including Uddiyana Bandha (navel contraction), the triple lock (Bandha-traya) forces Prana into the Sushumna Nadi. The Bhashya emphasizes that while Jihva Bandha is the supreme shortcut for those initiated by a Guru, for others, the triple lock is mandatory. It warns that Mula Bandha, if practiced incorrectly, causes physical ailments (dhatu-kshaya), whereas correct practice results in bodily health, digestive fire (agni), and the manifestation of inner sound (nada).

commentaries.description: भाष्य स्पष्ट करता है कि 'कण्ठसङ्कोचने' का अर्थ जालन्धरबन्ध है। 'अधस्तात् कुञ्चनेन' का अर्थ मूलबन्ध है। उड्डियानबन्ध के साथ मिलकर ये बन्धत्रय प्राण को सुषुम्ना नाडी में प्रविष्ट कराते हैं। भाष्य के अनुसार, यदि श्रीगुरु से जिह्वाबन्ध ज्ञात हो, तो वही पर्याप्त है। अन्यथा, बन्धत्रय आवश्यक है। मूलबन्ध के गलत अभ्यास से धातुक्षय और अन्य रोग होते हैं, जबकि सही अभ्यास से धातुपुष्टि, मलशुद्धि, अग्निदीप्ति और नादाभिव्यक्ति होती है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Bandha-traya (The Three Locks in Hatha Yoga)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse describes the foundational physical methodology for diverting the Prana into the Sushumna Nadi through the synergy of Mula Bandha (pelvic floor contraction) and Jalandhara Bandha (throat lock). This synchronization is considered essential for pranic regulation and spiritual ascent.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This remains a fundamental pedagogical pillar in traditional Hatha Yoga, distinguishing between mechanical practice and authentic transmission (Guru-mukha) to avoid physical imbalances.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed: Mula Bandha, Uddiyana Bandha, Jalandhara Bandha, and the advanced Jihva Bandha (Khechari-related component).
commentary_faqs.answer: Bandha-traya (Mula, Uddiyana, and Jalandhara) as instruments for the Nadi-shodhana and Prana-nirodha of the Sushumna Nadi.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Provides a psychological framework for the somatic regulation of the autonomic nervous system and stresses the importance of guided supervision in psycho-physical exercises to prevent negative outcomes.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description:
अपानमिति । अपानम् अपानवायुम् ऊर्ध्वमुत्थाप्य आधाराकुञ्चनेन प्राणं प्राणवायुं कण्ठादधः अधोभागे नयेत् प्रापयेत् यः सः योगी, योगः अस्य अस्ति, अभ्यस्यत्वेन इति योगी योगाभ्यासी जरया वार्धकेन विमुक्तः विशेषेण मुक्तः सन् । षोडशानामब्दानां समाहारः षोडशाब्दं वयो यस्य स तादृशो भवेत् । यद्यपि ‘पूरकान्ते तु कर्तव्यः’(५.४५) इत्यादिना त्रयाणां श्लोकानाम् एक एव अर्थः पर्यवस्यति, तथापि पूरकान्ते तु कर्तव्य इत्यनेन बन्धानां काल उक्तः । अधस्तात् कुञ्चनेन इत्यनेन बन्धानां स्वरूपमुक्तम् । अपानमूर्ध्वमुत्थाप्य इत्यनेन बन्धानां फलमुक्तमिति विशेषः । जालन्धरबन्धे मूलबन्धे च कृते नाभेरधोभाग आकर्षणाख्यः बन्ध उड्डियानबन्धो भवत्येव इत्यस्मिन् श्लोके नोक्तः । तथोचोक्तं ज्ञानेश्वरेण गीताषष्ठाध्यायव्याख्यायां -‘मूलबन्धे जालन्धरबन्धे च कृते नाभेरधोभाग आकर्षणाख्यः बन्धः स्वयमेव भवति ’ इति ॥ ४७ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: The commentary explains that by contracting the base (Mulabandha), one raises the Apana Vayu. Simultaneously, by drawing the Prana Vayu down from the throat (Jalandhara Bandha), the yogi transcends the effects of aging, effectively rejuvenating the body to a state of youthful vitality (symbolized as a sixteen-year-old). It notes that while this verse, along with others, describes the timing and method of Bandhas, it specifically focuses on the result of the practice—the union of breaths—which naturally leads to the engagement of the Uddiyana Bandha as well.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Energy Manipulation (Bandhas)
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse describes the yogic process of internalizing and uniting opposing vital currents to achieve metabolic and spiritual regulation. By reversing the natural directions of Apana and Prana, the practitioner creates an internal pressure that facilitates the awakening of subtle energies.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This is a cornerstone of Hatha Yoga practice, utilized to cleanse the subtle channels (nadis) and prepare the body for higher meditative states, highlighting the mastery of physiology through disciplined breath control.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practices prescribed include Mulabandha (root lock), Jalandhara Bandha (throat lock), and the subsequent, natural emergence of Uddiyana Bandha (abdominal lock) to achieve physiological rejuvenation.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around 'Prana-Apana Samyoga' (the union of Prana and Apana) facilitated by the 'Bandha-traya' (the three locks) which results in 'Jara-vimukti' (liberation from aging).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the integration of divergent mental and emotional energies. Secularly, it is recognized as a profound method for autonomic nervous system regulation and stress reduction through vagal stimulation.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Brahmananda)
commentaries.description:
‘योगाभ्यासक्रमं वक्ष्ये योगिनां योगसिद्धये ।
गुरुं संस्मृत्य शिरसि हृदये स्वेष्टदेवताम् ।
शुचौ देशे मठे रम्ये प्रतिष्ठाप्यासनं मृदु ।
देशकालौ च सङ्कीर्त्य सङ्कल्य विधिपूर्वकम् । ’
अद्येत्यादि श्रीपरमेश्वरप्रसादपूर्वकम् । समाधितत्फलसिध्यर्थम् आसनपूर्वकान् प्राणायामादीन् करिष्ये ।
मणिभ्राजद्फणासहस्रविधृतविश्वम्भरामण्डलायानन्ताय नागराजाय नमः ।
ततोऽभ्यसेदासनानि श्रमे जाते शवासनम् ।
करणीं विपरीताख्यां कुम्भकात् पूर्वमभ्यसेत् ।
विधायाचमनं कृत्वा कर्माङ्गं प्राणसंयमम् ।
कूर्मपुराणे शिववाक्यम् -
‘नमस्कृत्याथ योगीन्द्रान् सशिष्यांश्च विनायकम् ।
बद्ध्वाभ्यासे सिद्धपीठं कुम्भकाबन्धपूर्वकम् ।
कार्या अशीतिपर्यन्तं कुम्भकाः सुसमाहितैः ।
अनुलोमविलोमाख्यमेतं प्राहुर्मनीषिणः ।
उज्जायिनं ततः कुर्यात् सीत्कारीं शीतलीं ततः ।
मुद्राः समभ्यसेद् बुद्ध्वा गुरुवक्त्राद् यथाक्रमम् ।
अभ्यासं सकलं कुर्यादीश्वरार्पणमादृतः ।
स्नत्वा समापयेन्नित्यं कर्म सङ्क्षेपतः सुधीः ।
क्रियेत योगिना पथ्यमपथ्यं न कदाचन ।
केचित् कर्पूरमिच्छन्ति ताम्बूलं शोभनं तथा ।
इति चिन्तामणेर्वाक्यं स्वारस्यं भजते न हि ।
भोजनान्तरं कुर्यान्मोक्षशास्त्रावलोकनम् ।
सायं सन्ध्याविधिं कृत्वा योगं पूर्ववदभ्यसेत् ।
अभ्यासानन्तरं कार्या सायं सन्ध्या सदा बुधैः ।
विपरीतां तु करणीं सायङ्कालार्धरात्रयोः ।
अथोद्देशानुक्रमेण कुम्भजान् विवक्षुः तत्र प्रथमोदितं सूर्यभेदनं तद्वुणांश्चाह त्रिभिः - आसन इति । सुखं ददातीति सुखदं तस्मिन् सुखदे ।
शुचौ देशे प्रतिष्ठाप्य स्थिरमासनमात्मनः ।
नात्युच्छ्रितं नातिनीचं चैलाजिनकुशोत्तरम् ॥ (भ.गी.६.११) इत्युक्तलक्षणे ‘विविक्तदेशे च सुखासनस्थः शुचिः समग्रीवशिरःशरीरः ’ (कै.उप.५) इति श्रुतेश्च चैलाजिनकुशोत्तर आसने । आस्ते अस्मिन् इति आसनम्, आस्यते अनेन इति वा तस्मिन् योगी योगाभ्यासी । आसनं स्वस्तिकवीरसिद्धपद्मादन्यतमं मुख्यत्वात् सिद्धासनमेव वा बद्ध्वा एव बन्धनेन संपाद्यैव कृत्वैव इत्यर्थः । तत आसनबन्धनन्तरं दक्षा दक्षिणभागस्था या नाडी पिङ्गला तया बहिःस्थं देहात् बहिर्वर्तमानं पवनं वायुं शनैः मन्दं मन्दमाकृष्य पिङ्गलया मन्दं मन्दं पूरकं कृत्वा इत्यर्थः ॥ ४८ ॥

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: The commentary explains that the Yogi, following a specific sequence—remembering the Guru, the presiding deity, and selecting a clean place—establishes a stable seat (āsana) according to the definitions in texts like the Bhagavad Gita and Kaivalya Upanishad. It clarifies that 'āsana' implies specific postures like Siddhasana, and the process involves drawing in the breath through the Pingala nadi after stabilization.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: टीका स्पष्ट करती है कि योगी गुरु, इष्टदेवता का स्मरण और पवित्र स्थान के चयन के पश्चात भगवद्गीता और कैवल्य उपनिषद में वर्णित लक्षणों के अनुरूप आसन की प्रतिष्ठा करता है। इसमें स्पष्ट किया गया है कि 'आसन' से तात्पर्य स्वस्तिक, वीर, सिद्ध या पद्मासन आदि से है, तथा आसनबद्ध होने के उपरांत पिंगला नाड़ी से प्राणवायु के पूरक की प्रक्रिया प्रारंभ होती है।
